development: Fertilization has happened; the zygote is dividing as it travels to the uterus.
Implantation begins late this week.
body_changes: You may feel nothing at all yet — that is normal.
Some women notice mild cramping or light spotting at implantation.
tips: Start (or continue) a prenatal vitamin with 400–800 mcg folic acid.
Avoid alcohol and smoking.

development: The embryo implants into the uterine lining.
hCG hormone begins rising — this is what pregnancy tests detect.
body_changes: Missed period.
Mild fatigue or breast tenderness may begin.
tips: Take a home pregnancy test if you haven't.
Book your first prenatal appointment (usually weeks 8–10).

development: The neural tube (future brain and spine) is forming.
The heart begins to beat.
body_changes: Nausea may start.
Frequent urination and fatigue are common.
tips: Eat small, frequent meals if nauseated.
Keep hydrating.

development: Heartbeat may be visible on ultrasound (~110 bpm).
Early facial features and arm/leg buds appear.
body_changes: Morning sickness often peaks in the coming weeks.
Food aversions or strong smells sensitivity.
tips: Ginger or plain crackers can ease nausea.
Rest when you can — fatigue is real.

development: Brain is growing rapidly.
Hands and feet are forming.
body_changes: Nausea may still be strong.
Breasts may feel fuller and tender.
tips: A comfortable bra helps.
Tell your provider about any medication you take.

development: Fingers are forming; the embryo begins small movements.
Major organs are in place.
body_changes: Bloating and mild cramping can occur.
Mood swings are common.
tips: First prenatal visit usually happens around now.
Write down questions for your provider.

development: Now officially called a fetus.
Muscles are developing; small movements continue.
body_changes: Nausea often near its peak.
Waistband may start to feel tight.
tips: Iron-rich foods help with fatigue.
Gentle walks are great.

development: Bones and cartilage are forming.
The fetus can kick and swallow.
body_changes: Some women feel slightly better this week.
Round-ligament twinges possible.
tips: Ask about NIPT/cell-free DNA screening (available from week 10).
Keep taking prenatal vitamins.

development: The fetus can open and close its fists.
External genitalia start differentiating.
body_changes: Nausea often begins to ease soon.
Skin changes may appear.
tips: Stay consistent with hydration.
Start thinking about first-trimester screening (weeks 11–13).

development: Reflexes are developing.
Heartbeat can sometimes be heard with a Doppler.
body_changes: End of trimester 1 is near — many symptoms improve.
Energy may start returning.
tips: First-trimester screening (nuchal translucency) is typically done weeks 11–13.
Share the news if you'd like to!

development: Unique fingerprints are forming.
Vocal cords are developing.
body_changes: Trimester 2 begins next week.
Bump may start showing slightly.
tips: Balanced meals with protein and fiber help energy.
Begin a gentle exercise routine if not already.

development: The fetus can make facial expressions.
Fine hair (lanugo) covers the body for warmth.
body_changes: Often called the 'honeymoon' phase — energy returns.
Round-ligament pain may appear as the uterus grows.
tips: Change positions slowly to ease round-ligament pain.
Plan the anatomy scan (~week 20) with your provider.

development: Senses are developing; light sensitivity begins.
The skeleton is hardening from cartilage to bone.
body_changes: Nasal stuffiness can occur.
Appetite often increases.
tips: Calcium-rich foods support bone development.
Start looking into prenatal classes if interested.

development: Ears are in position; hearing begins to develop.
The umbilical cord is fully formed.
body_changes: You may feel more comfortable than in trimester 1.
First flutters of movement may come soon (often weeks 16–20).
tips: Note any first movements for your records.
Keep up regular check-ups.
